page.h1: HTS Chapter 08: Edible Fruit and Nuts — Export Markets & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Goods

seo.title: Chapter 08 Export Markets: Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Fruit & Nuts
seo.shortDescription: What Canada, the EU, India, Mexico, Viet Nam, Korea, Japan, the UAE and China charge on U.S. almonds, pistachios, walnuts and fresh fruit in 2026, and the approval each one needs.

intro: What each large market charges on U.S. fruit and nuts in 2026, next to what the U.S. shipped there in 2025; the EU counts as one market because its members share one tariff. China is added at the end, although it is no longer a top buyer, because it is the one market charging U.S. goods an extra duty. For most of the trade tariffs are low: Canada and Mexico charge nothing under USMCA, South Korea almost nothing under KORUS, the EU nothing on nuts within its U.S. quota, and Japan nothing on most nuts, oranges and cherries. India (on almonds and apples) and China cost real money. For fresh fruit, the buyer’s plant-health rules usually decide whether a fruit can be sold at all.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

profile.headline: Canada is by far the largest buyer, mostly of fresh fruit (berries, bananas, grapes, avocados and citrus), all duty-free under CUSMA. Its March–September 2025 counter-tariff did hit U.S. citrus, peaches, watermelons, pecans and frozen berries, but it ended on September 1, 2025, and its September 2026 counter-tariffs skip fruit and nuts.
profile.mainProducts: Other fresh fruit (berries, kiwifruit, tropical fruit) (0810) · Bananas & plantains (0803)

regulator.name: Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA)
regulator.requirement: The importer needs a Safe Food for Canadians licence. CFIA's Automated Import Reference System (AIRS) sets the plant-health conditions for each fruit and U.S. origin; some need a USDA phytosanitary certificate.

profile.headline: The EU buys U.S. tree nuts, mainly almonds, through Germany, Spain, the Netherlands and Italy. Since July 1, 2026 U.S. tree nuts enter duty-free within a 500,000-tonne yearly quota and several dried fruits are duty-free; to claim the preference the importer must prove U.S. origin (document code U190).
profile.mainProducts: Other nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, pistachios, pecans…) (0802) · Dried fruit (prunes, apricots…) & mixtures (0813)
profile.tariffNow: Nuts free within U.S. quota; fresh-fruit % duty removed (July 2026)

regulator.name: European Commission (DG SANTE) and member-state border control posts
regulator.requirement: Fresh fruit needs a USDA phytosanitary certificate under EU plant-health rules. Nuts need none, but must meet EU aflatoxin limits at the border, so shippers send USDA-run PEC (almonds) or PEAR (pistachios) test results.

profile.headline: Viet Nam is the fastest-growing buyer, up 59% in 2025, mostly of in-shell pistachios and almonds. Its March 2025 decree cut tariffs on shelled almonds, in-shell pistachios, apples, cherries and raisins to 5%, and the October 2025 U.S.–Viet Nam framework promises preferential access for substantially all U.S. farm goods, with no rates published yet.

assumptions: Rates are each market's 2026 schedule: Canada's and Mexico's USMCA schedules, Korea's KORUS schedule, Japan's Tariff Schedule of April 1, 2026, the EU Common Customs Tariff with Regulation (EU) 2026/1455, Viet Nam's Decree 26/2023 as amended by Decree 73/2025, India's customs tariff, and the GCC common tariff for the UAE.

Each cell names the products that carry most of the trade in that group (for nuts: almonds, pistachios, walnuts); other lines in the same heading can pay a different rate. Cells marked "not individually verified" are small groups where the rate was not checked line by line.
Trade-agreement rates apply only to goods that meet the agreement’s rules of origin; the EU’s 2026 U.S. preferences need proof of U.S. origin. Quota rates apply only while the quota lasts.

China's cells add its 15% 2018 counter-tariff and its extra 10% on all U.S. goods to its normal rate. Its 2018–19 counter-tariffs answering U.S. Section 301 (25% or more on fruit and nuts) are waived only for buyers holding an exclusion, valid until December 31, 2026; they are not included in the cells.
National 8–10-digit tariff lines can set a different rate than the six-digit subheading. Check the market's own schedule before relying on this page for a transaction.
